title: Pali, closed
hook: back from a month abroad with thank you, sorry and a bus stop: what is a little of a language worth?
tomorrow: a monk says he wrote a poem only for himself. so why read it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a full chant: the bow, the refuges, the five trainings, strung together, the shape holding your place. The whole chant. Today the block closes.

Someone comes home from a month abroad and can't order a full meal in the language. But they can say thank you, and sorry, and the name of their bus stop, and the woman at the bakery smiles every time. That's not fluency. It isn't nothing, either. Twenty-nine days of Pali come to something like that. So, one question to close the block: what is a little of an old language actually worth?
screen: `THANK YOU, SORRY, A BUS STOP.` → `NOT FLUENCY. NOT NOTHING.` → `WHAT IS A LITTLE WORTH?`

segments.voice: The tradition's answer starts where this block did. When two monks asked to put the teaching into grand verse, the Buddha said no: learn it in your own dialect. Meaning comes first. So Pali isn't a password. It's a shared door, the tongue the chants live in, so a girl from a Vietnamese family can chant beside Lao kids and Thai grandparents and all of them land on the same word. Look what's behind that door now: namo, homage; saranam, refuge; sikkhapada, a training taken up. The heart in Pali. Come and see. Thus indeed is he. Practicing well. Skilled in good. The highest blessing. Thus have I heard. Sadhu. Strive on with care. A little Pali. Now a neighbor. A Muslim friend who grew up speaking Urdu or English or Malay may still say alhamdulillah, praise be to God, after a meal or a sneeze or good news. It comes from the Qur'an's opening chapter, in Pickthall's words: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." A few old words, carried into ordinary days by people of different mother tongues. That's shared. And one honest difference. Muslims hold the Qur'an's Arabic to be God's own revealed word, which is why recitation keeps it. In the Pali story, the Buddha let his words go out in any dialect, and Buddhism names no God speaking them. Same door-sized words. Different houses behind them.
screen: `LEARN IT IN YOUR OWN DIALECT.` · `PALI: A SHARED DOOR.` · `ALHAMDULILLAH: PRAISE BE TO GOD.` · `GOD'S OWN WORD, OR ANY DIALECT.` · then, large: `A LITTLE PALI.`

segments.voice: Chant the homage once more, slowly: namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa. Then listen to the quiet right after it, the way a bell's sound thins out. Stay with that one sound until it's gone, and then with the stillness.
Pali: the language of the Theravada chants and canon. Not a password; a shared door, learned a few words at a time.
The line to keep: a little Pali, a door that opens onto people. The block is complete.

screen: `DAY 1455 COUNTS.` → `A LITTLE PALI · 29 OF 29.` → `TOMORROW: A POEM HE WROTE ONLY FOR HIMSELF. WHY READ IT?`

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Laos and beyond chant in Pali while speaking their own languages at home; new chanters learn by ear, a few words at a time, sometimes from sheets with a translation alongside.
